title: Logging Architecture & the Sidecar Pattern 🪵
description: Master kubectl logs, use sidecar containers to ship logs, and understand the EFK stack.

slides.title: Kubernetes Logging 101 📜
slides.content:
# Containers write to stdout/stderr

By default, Kubernetes captures everything a container writes to stdout and stderr. These logs are stored on the node and accessible via `kubectl logs`.

- `kubectl logs <pod>` – standard output of the first container.
- `kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>` – specific container.
- `kubectl logs -f <pod>` – follow.
- `kubectl logs --previous <pod>` – previous crashed instance.

But logs are **not persistent**: when a Pod is deleted, its logs are gone unless you ship them elsewhere.

quizData.question: True or False: `kubectl logs` will always show logs of a Pod even after it has been deleted.
quizData.explanation: Logs are stored on the node and deleted when the Pod is removed or log rotation occurs.

slides.title: The Sidecar Logging Pattern 🧑‍🤝‍🧑
slides.content:
# Ship logs with a helper container

If your app writes logs to a file (not stdout), you can use a sidecar container that reads the file and outputs it to its own stdout. This way `kubectl logs` works, or a logging agent can pick them up.

Example: app writes to `/var/log/app.log`. A sidecar container runs `tail -f /var/log/app.log`. Both share an emptyDir volume.

slides.title: Sidecar Logging Example
slides.codeSnippet:
containers:
- name: app
  image: my-app
  volumeMounts:
  - name: logs
    mountPath: /var/log
- name: log-sidecar
  image: busybox
  command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -f /var/log/app.log"]
  volumeMounts:
  - name: logs
    mountPath: /var/log
volumes:
- name: logs
  emptyDir: {}

quizData.question: What is a typical use of a sidecar container for logging?

options.text: To read log files and forward them to stdout or a collector

quizData.explanation: Sidecars act as log shippers, converting file‑based logs to stdout or sending to external systems.

slides.title: Centralized Logging with EFK/ELK 📚
slides.content:
# Search, analyze, visualize

For production, you need a centralized logging system:
- **Elasticsearch** – stores and indexes logs.
- **Fluentd/Fluent Bit** – collects and forwards logs from nodes.
- **Kibana** – web UI to search and visualize logs.

Alternatively, **Loki** (by Grafana) is a lightweight, Prometheus‑like logging system that integrates with Grafana.

How it works:
1. Fluentd runs as a DaemonSet on every node, tailing container logs.
2. It enriches logs with Kubernetes metadata (Pod name, namespace, labels).
3. Sends to Elasticsearch.
4. Kibana queries Elasticsearch and provides dashboards.

slides.title: Deploying EFK with Helm ⛵
slides.content:
## Quick installation

```bash
helm repo add elastic https://helm.elastic.co
helm install elasticsearch elastic/elasticsearch -n logging --create-namespace
helm install fluentd fluent/fluentd -n logging
helm install kibana elastic/kibana -n logging
```

Then access Kibana:
```bash
kubectl port-forward svc/kibana-kibana 5601 -n logging
```

quizData.question: Which component in the EFK stack collects logs from nodes?
quizData.explanation: Fluentd/Fluent Bit runs as a node‑level log agent, forwarding logs to Elasticsearch.

slides.title: Loki – The Lighter Alternative 🦎
slides.content:
## From Grafana Labs

Loki is designed to be cost‑effective and easy to operate. It indexes only metadata (labels), not full text, and stores compressed chunks. It integrates with Grafana seamlessly.

Deploy with:
```bash
helm install loki grafana/loki-stack -n monitoring
```

It includes Promtail (log collector) and Loki. Great for teams already using Grafana.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Always include a timestamp and structured fields in logs

Use JSON logging format – it makes querying in Elasticsearch or Loki much easier. Include fields like `timestamp`, `level`, `service`, `trace_id`.
